spans.s:
cosmology
------------------------------------------
This world in which we live, move, and have our being as it were, has been spurring the imagination of philosophers for millennia, about its origin and evolution. It will be an interesting, nay, even fascinating, experience to go through the various accounts of च्रेअतिओन् given in the Hindu scriptures and philosophical works.
The ऋग्वेद had dealt with this subject in a few hymns but there is no attempt at giving a cogent theory and well-reasoned philosophy. Before सृष्टि or च्रेअतिओन्, Deva or God alone existed. He is our ड़थेर्. He desired to create. He manifested this world out of himself and entered into it (vide ऋग्वेद 10.81.1; 10.5.7). The famous पुरुषसूक्त (Ṛgveda 10.90) describes the whole च्रेअतिओन् as having come out of the पुरुष or primeval Being, using the allegory of a sacrifice.
Allied Vedic works like the ब्राह्मणस् hold similar views. The Taitti-rīya ब्राह्मण by implication declares (2.8.9.7) that the Deva is both the material and the efficient cause of this universe. The words ‘Viśvakarmā’ (one, whose work this world is), ‘Hiraṇyagarbha’ (golden egg) and ‘Prajāpati’ (lord of beings) have also been used in this work to denote the Creator.
In some of the Vedic accounts of च्रेअतिओन्, primeval waters form the first product from which subsequent च्रेअतिओन् takes place. We thus see two streams of thought here: one advocating evolution of the world from God and the other, च्रेअतिओन् by God. Accounts of च्रेअतिओन् usually contain accounts of sustenance and dissolution (sthiti and प्रलय) also.
The उपनिषद्स् which contain more specific references to च्रेअतिओन्, generally follow the Vedic thought pattern. Before च्रेअतिओन्, ब्रह्मन्, also called आत्मन् or Sat, alone existed. It desired to become many and created तेजस् or fire, ap or water and अन्न or earth. They are the three fundamental elements from which the whole च्रेअतिओन् came out (vide छान्दोग्य उपनिषद् 6.2). Some other उपनिषद्स् trace the evolution of the world from the आत्मन् through the पञ्चभूतस् or five fundamental elements (vide तैत्तिरीय उपनिषद् 2.1; 2.6) and others like the Praśna (1.4), through the च्रेअतिओन् of matter and spirit (rayi and प्राण). There are also accounts according to which the individual souls have sprung from ब्रह्मन् like sparks from the fire (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad

). The idea that ब्रह्मन्, having created the world, has entered into it and controls it from within, is also advocated (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).
The epics and the पुराणस् give their own, variegated, accounts of च्रेअतिओन्. In one pattern of descriptions, विष्णु or नारायण brings forth ब्रह्मा (the four-faced creator) who subsequently creates the various worlds (numbering 3 or 7 or even 14) and their denizens out of himself. In another set of descriptions, नारायण creates a golden egg (Hiraṇyagarbha) which starts floating on the primeval waters. He himself animates it, breaks it into two, forming the earth and हेअवेन्. The पुरुष or प्रजापति that comes out of it then creates all beings. The Creator dividing himself into two, the male and the female principles, and their union giving rise to the whole च्रेअतिओन् is also found in some descriptions. In fact this theory is based on similar descriptions found in उपनिषद्स् like the Bṛhadā-raṇyaka (

-4).
The षड्-दर्शनस् or the six philosophical systems, also discuss this question and give their own theories. The न्याय and Vaiśeṣika schools state that ईश्वर or God creates the world out of the eternal substances like atoms, space, time, ether, मिन्द् and souls. He is also responsible for the sustenance and dissolution of the world. The Sāṅkhya and the योग systems posit the theory that प्रकृति or primeval nature (consisting of the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्) evolves by stages into this world due to the will of ईश्वर (God) and the presence of the puruṣas or individual souls. This theory is echoed in some of the पुराणस् also. The Pūrva-mīmāṁsā system considers the world and souls to be eternally there—neither created nor destroyed—but regulated by कर्म (unseen effects of actions done).
The Vedānta system just organizes the philosophy of the उपनिषद्स्. The Advaita Vedānta of शङ्कर (A.

-820) considers the world as an illusory appearance in ब्रह्मन्, the real substratum. Though the general theory of च्रेअतिओन् given in the उपनिषद्स् is accepted, it is given only an empirical status. The theistic schools of Vedānta, of Rāmānuja (A.

-1276) on the other hand, accept the reality of च्रेअतिओन् and the created world.
It is thus seen that there are so many varieties and types of description of the च्रेअतिओन् process that it is difficult to put forward any definite theories. However, the thought pattern revealed in the ऋग्वेद and developed in the उपनिषद्स् may be treated as more authentic and more universally accepted than others. Summarized briefly, it states that God the Absolute, creates the world out of himself, out of his own will, sustains it and rules over it, and dissolves it at the end of a cycle. This cycle of च्रेअतिओन्, sustenance and dissolution goes on eternally.
The whole purpose of च्रेअतिओन् is to give the jīvas or the individual souls in bondage, one more chance for redemption and लिबेरतिओन् from transmigration. This being the main theme of Hindu philosophy and religion, it has not paid much attention to the details of the process of च्रेअतिओन्.
